stem: Half life of \(^{18}\mathrm{F}\) is 110 minutes. What fraction of \(^{18}\mathrm{F}\) sample decays in 20 minutes?
our_solution:
Given: \(t_{1/2} = 110\) min, \(t = 20\) min.

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{110\ \mathrm{min}} = 6.30 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — fraction remaining.** From Eq. (13.9), \(\log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{\lambda t}{2.303}\):

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{6.30 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{min^{-1}} \times 20\ \mathrm{min}}{2.303} = \dfrac{0.126}{2.303} = 0.0547\)

\(\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \mathrm{antilog}\ (0.0547) = 1.1343\)

\(\dfrac{N}{N_0} = \dfrac{1}{1.1343} = 0.8816\)

**Step 3 — fraction decayed.**

fraction decayed \(= 1 - \dfrac{N}{N_0} = 1 - 0.8816 = 0.118\)

**About 0.118, that is 11.8 %, of the \(^{18}\mathrm{F}\) sample decays in 20 minutes.** (The answer is a fraction and so has no unit.)

stem: Half life of \(^{35}\mathrm{S}\) is 87.8 d. What percentage of \(^{35}\mathrm{S}\) sample remains after 180 d?
our_solution:
Given: \(t_{1/2} = 87.8\) d, \(t = 180\) d. Take \(N_0 = 100\).

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{87.8\ \mathrm{d}} = 7.893 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — apply the rate law.**

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{\lambda t}{2.303} = \dfrac{7.893 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times 180\ \mathrm{d}}{2.303} = \dfrac{1.4207}{2.303} = 0.6169\)

\(\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \mathrm{antilog}\ (0.6169) = 4.139\)

**Step 3 — percentage remaining.**

\(N = \dfrac{100}{4.139} = 24.2\)

**24.2 % of the \(^{35}\mathrm{S}\) sample remains after 180 days.**

(As a check, 180 d is a little over two half lives, and two half lives would leave 25 %.)

stem: Half life \(^{67}\mathrm{Ga}\) is 78 h. How long will it take to decay 12% of sample of Ga?
our_solution:
Given: \(t_{1/2} = 78\) h. 12 % of the sample decays, so 88 % remains: take \(N_0 = 100\) and \(N = 88\).

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{78\ \mathrm{h}} = 8.885 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — apply the rate law.** From \(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N}\),

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{\lambda}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{100}{88} = \dfrac{2.303}{8.885 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{h^{-1}}} \times \log_{10}(1.1364)\)

\(= 259.2\ \mathrm{h} \times 0.05552 = 14.4\ \mathrm{h}\)

**It takes about 14.4 hours for 12 % of the \(^{67}\mathrm{Ga}\) sample to decay.**

(The unit is hours, since the half life was given in hours; the printed answer 14.44 omits the unit and differs only in the fourth figure, from rounding of the logarithm.)

stem: 0.5 g Sample of \(^{201}\mathrm{Tl}\) decays to 0.0788 g in 8 days. What is its half life?
our_solution:
Given: \(N_0 = 0.5\) g, \(N = 0.0788\) g, \(t = 8\) days. (Masses may be used in place of numbers of nuclei, since the two are proportional for one isotope.)

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{2.303}{8\ \mathrm{d}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{0.5}{0.0788}\)

\(= 0.28788\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times \log_{10}(6.345) = 0.28788\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times 0.80252 = 0.2310\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — half life.**

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.2310\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}} = 3.0\ \mathrm{d}\)

**The half life of \(^{201}\mathrm{Tl}\) is 3.0 days.**

(Check: 8 days is close to \(2\tfrac{2}{3}\) half lives, and \(0.5/2^{8/3} = 0.0787\) g, which is the mass given.)

stem: 65% of \(^{111}\mathrm{In}\) sample decays in 4.2 d. What is its half life?
our_solution:
Given: 65 % of the sample decays in 4.2 d, so 35 % remains. Take \(N_0 = 100\), \(N = 35\), \(t = 4.2\) d.

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{2.303}{4.2\ \mathrm{d}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{100}{35}\)

\(= 0.54833\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times \log_{10}(2.857) = 0.54833\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times 0.45593 = 0.2500\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — half life.**

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.2500\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}} = 2.77\ \mathrm{d}\)

**The half life of \(^{111}\mathrm{In}\) is 2.77 days.**

stem: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of \(^{84}_{36}\mathrm{Kr}\) whose atomic mass is 83.913 u. (Mass of neutron is 1.0087 u and that of H atom is 1.0078 u).
our_solution:
For \(^{84}_{36}\mathrm{Kr}\): \(Z = 36\), \(A = 84\), so \(A - Z = 48\) neutrons. \(m = 83.913\) u.

**Step 1 — mass defect,** using Eq. (13.2), \(\Delta m = [Z m_{\mathrm{H}} + (A - Z) m_{\mathrm{n}}] - m\):

\(\Delta m = [36 \times 1.0078\ \mathrm{u} + 48 \times 1.0087\ \mathrm{u}] - 83.913\ \mathrm{u}\)

\(= [36.2808 + 48.4176]\ \mathrm{u} - 83.913\ \mathrm{u} = 84.6984\ \mathrm{u} - 83.913\ \mathrm{u} = 0.7854\ \mathrm{u}\)

**Step 2 — total binding energy,** using Eq. (13.3):

\(\mathrm{B.E.} = \Delta m\ (\mathrm{u}) \times 931.4 = 0.7854 \times 931.4 = 731.5\ \mathrm{MeV}\)

**Step 3 — binding energy per nucleon,** using Eq. (13.4):

\(\overline{B} = \dfrac{\mathrm{B.E.}}{A} = \dfrac{731.5\ \mathrm{MeV}}{84} = 8.71\ \mathrm{MeV\ per\ nucleon}\)

**The binding energy per nucleon of \(^{84}\mathrm{Kr}\) is about 8.7 MeV.**

stem:
Calculate the energy in Mev released in the nuclear reaction

\(^{174}_{77}\mathrm{Ir} \longrightarrow {}^{170}_{75}\mathrm{Re} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\)

Atomic masses : Ir = 173.97 u, Re = 169.96 u and He = 4.0026 u
our_solution:
**Step 1 — mass defect of the reaction.** The energy released comes from the mass lost in going from reactant to products:

\(\Delta m = \text{mass of } ^{174}\mathrm{Ir} - (\text{mass of } ^{170}\mathrm{Re} + \text{mass of } ^{4}\mathrm{He})\)

\(= 173.97\ \mathrm{u} - (169.96\ \mathrm{u} + 4.0026\ \mathrm{u})\)

\(= 173.97\ \mathrm{u} - 173.9626\ \mathrm{u} = 0.0074\ \mathrm{u}\)

**Step 2 — convert the mass loss to energy,** using \(1\ \mathrm{u} \equiv 931.4\) MeV:

\(E = \Delta m\ (\mathrm{u}) \times 931.4 = 0.0074 \times 931.4 = 6.89\ \mathrm{MeV}\)

**The energy released in the reaction is 6.89 MeV.**

(\(\Delta m\) is positive, so mass is lost and energy is RELEASED, as it must be for a spontaneous \(\alpha\)-decay.)

stem: A 3/4 of the original amount of radioisotope decays in 60 minutes. What is its half life?
our_solution:
If \(3/4\) of the original amount has decayed, then the amount REMAINING is

\(1 - \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{1}{4}\) of the original.

By the definition of half life, each half life halves the amount remaining:

\(N_0 \xrightarrow{\ t_{1/2}\ } \dfrac{N_0}{2} \xrightarrow{\ t_{1/2}\ } \dfrac{N_0}{4}\)

So reaching one quarter takes **two** half lives, and those two half lives occupy 60 minutes:

\(2\ t_{1/2} = 60\ \mathrm{min}\), hence \(t_{1/2} = 30\ \mathrm{min}\)

**The half life of the radioisotope is 30 minutes.**

(The same result follows from the rate law: \(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{60\ \mathrm{min}}\log_{10} 4 = 0.0231\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\), and \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/0.0231 = 30\) min.)

stem: How many - particles are emitted by 0.1 g of \(^{226}\mathrm{Ra}\) in one year?
our_solution:
The number of particles emitted in a given time is the **activity** of the sample, \(-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N\). Radium-226 is an \(\alpha\)-emitter — section 13.6.1 gives its decay as \(^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} \longrightarrow {}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}\) — so the particles counted are \(\alpha\)-particles.

**Step 1 — decay constant.** The stem does not give the half life; Table 13.4 (b) of this chapter gives \(t_{1/2} = 1620\) y for radium-226.

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{1620\ \mathrm{y}} = 4.278 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — number of nuclei in 0.1 g.**

\(N = \dfrac{0.1\ \mathrm{g}}{226\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}} = 2.665 \times 10^{20}\) nuclei

**Step 3 — activity.**

\(-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N = 4.278 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}} \times 2.665 \times 10^{20} = 1.14 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\)

**About \(1.14 \times 10^{17}\) \(\alpha\)-particles are emitted in one year.**

[Note: the stem prints "How many - particles", with the particle symbol missing before the hyphen, and it does not state the half life. The printed answer \(1.154 \times 10^{17}\) is what \(t_{1/2} = 1600\) y would give; the chapter's own Table 13.4 (b) says 1620 y, which gives the \(1.14 \times 10^{17}\) above. The two differ only by the half life used.]

stem: A sample of \(^{32}\mathrm{P}\) initially shows activity of one Curie. After 303 days the activity falls to \(1.5 \times 10^{4}\) dps. What is the half life of \(^{32}\mathrm{P}\)?
our_solution:
**Step 1 — put both activities in the same unit.** Section 13.5.6 gives \(1\ \mathrm{Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\) dps, so the initial activity is

\(-\dfrac{dN_0}{dt} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{dps}\), and after 303 days \(-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = 1.5 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{dps}\).

Since activity is proportional to the number of nuclei, the ratio of activities equals \(N_0/N\).

**Step 2 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{2.303}{303\ \mathrm{d}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{3.7 \times 10^{10}}{1.5 \times 10^{4}}\)

\(= 7.601 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times \log_{10}(2.467 \times 10^{6})\)

\(= 7.601 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} \times 6.392 = 0.04858\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

**Step 3 — half life.**

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.04858\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}} = 14.27\ \mathrm{d}\)

**The half life of \(^{32}\mathrm{P}\) is 14.27 days.**

stem: Half life of radon is 3.82 d. By what time would 99.9 % of radon will be decayed.
our_solution:
Given: \(t_{1/2} = 3.82\) d. If 99.9 % has decayed, 0.1 % remains: take \(N_0 = 100\) and \(N = 100 - 99.9 = 0.1\).

**Step 1 — decay constant.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{3.82\ \mathrm{d}} = 0.18141\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — time required.**

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{\lambda}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{2.303}{0.18141\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{100}{0.1}\)

\(= 12.695\ \mathrm{d} \times \log_{10}(1000) = 12.695\ \mathrm{d} \times 3 = 38.1\ \mathrm{d}\)

**Radon will be 99.9 % decayed after about 38.1 days**, that is roughly 10 half lives (\(2^{10} = 1024 \approx 1000\)).

stem: It has been found that the Sun's mass loss is \(4.34 \times 10^{9}\) kg per second. How much energy per second would be radiated into space by the Sun?
our_solution:
The Sun radiates energy because it loses mass, and the two are connected by Einstein's equation \(E = mc^{2}\) (section 13.3.5).

Given: \(m = 4.34 \times 10^{9}\) kg lost per second, \(c = 3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}\).

\(E = mc^{2} = 4.34 \times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{kg} \times (3 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}})^{2}\)

\(= 4.34 \times 10^{9} \times 9 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(= 3.906 \times 10^{26}\ \mathrm{J}\)

Converting to kilojoules,

\(E = \dfrac{3.906 \times 10^{26}}{10^{3}}\ \mathrm{kJ} = 3.9 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

**The Sun radiates about \(3.9 \times 10^{23}\) kJ into space every second**, that is \(3.9 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{kJ\ s^{-1}}\). This energy is the result of the nuclear fusion reactions taking place in the Sun.

stem: A sample of old wood shows 7.0 dps/g. If the fresh sample of tree shows 16.0 dps/g, How old is the given sample of wood? Half life of \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\) 5730 y.
our_solution:
This is radiocarbon dating (section 13.8.1). The fresh sample gives the activity the wood had at the moment the tree died, so \(N_0 = 16.0\) dps/g and \(N = 7.0\) dps/g.

**Step 1 — decay constant of \(^{14}\mathrm{C}\).**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{5730\ \mathrm{y}} = 1.21 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — age of the sample.**

\(t = \dfrac{2.303}{\lambda}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{2.303}{1.21 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}}\ \log_{10}\dfrac{16.0}{7.0}\)

\(= 1.9033 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{y} \times \log_{10}(2.2857)\)

\(= 1.9033 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{y} \times 0.35908 = 6833\ \mathrm{y}\)

**The wood sample is about 6833 years old.**

(The answer is an age, so the unit is YEARS; the chapter's own rounded value \(\lambda = 1.21 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{y^{-1}}\) has been used, and carrying \(0.693/5730\) unrounded gives 6837 y.)
